title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.

items.label: Solar eclipse
points: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
The Moon's shadow falls on Earth

items.label: Lunar eclipse
points: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
Earth's shadow falls on the Moon

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. That's why, during a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow.

cards.headline: Eclipses: explained
learned: Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun
Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The 400× coincidence makes total solar eclipses possible

questions.prompt: During a lunar eclipse, what is happening?

options.label: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon enters its new phase

questions.explanation: In a lunar eclipse Earth sits between the Sun and the Moon, and its shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.prompt: Why can the Moon exactly cover the Sun during a total solar eclipse?

options.label: The Moon and Sun are actually the same size
options.rationale: The Sun is about 400 times wider.

options.label: The Moon is closer to the Sun
The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther away

questions.explanation: The Sun's extra size is balanced by its extra distance, so both look about the same size from Earth.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: why can a lunar eclipse only happen at full Moon?

options.label: The Moon is always closest to Earth at full Moon
options.rationale: The Moon’s distance doesn’t follow its phases.

options.label: Full Moons are brighter, so eclipses show up
The Moon briefly stops orbiting at full Moon
Only then does Earth sit between the Sun and Moon

questions.explanation: At full Moon, Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. When the three line up exactly, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
